question.problem:
Solve the initial value problem
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118626/assets/ea0084a8b024c1b1680e34a3ff3d395f166de655db503bd3f9415c23be24a5f1.svg)

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is $\lambda_1=3+\textrm{i}.$*
question.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118626/assets/e49a5731becdf1c7c11904a9da6407a9ef75e3af91e278590ececdab49b618c7.svg) 

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda_1=3+\textrm{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For $\lambda_1 =3+\textrm{i},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118626/assets/fba3794fb2b0767d7f221dc766636f51a1ffe06fd529ab1423df74aeae2b9db6.svg)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118626/assets/6e16f0e74bf298c51302325450383ff3edf67912994c6604d22a3bbca1c292bd.svg)

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = \overline{\lambda}_1$ is 
$\mathbf{v}_2 = \overline{\mathbf{v}}_1.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = 3 + \textrm{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118626/assets/43419fd3567cb18d8132bdc6e12a204efe946280f83593056394d588b07cc71b.svg)

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf w_1$ and $\mathbf w_2$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial condition ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118626/assets/f61dd79b0a32acd6788f4f4f27e7438c52612b59266145af08b79d38687dd170.svg) Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}-3[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$
